turns.message: How does this compare with my other 70.3?
turns.reply:
You were faster across the board at Ridgeline than at Coastal, and the run is where the gap really opened up.

Ridgeline 70.3 beat Coastal 70.3 by 10 minutes 50 seconds overall. Breaking it down: swim was 50 seconds faster, T1 10 seconds faster, bike 5 minutes 10 seconds faster, T2 10 seconds faster, and the run was 4 minutes 30 seconds faster. So the bike and run each contributed meaningfully to the improvement, with the bike being the single biggest chunk of time gained and the run close behind.

The rankings back this up too — Ridgeline placed you Top 11% overall and Top 9% in your age group, both better than Coastal's Top 15% overall and Top 14% age group.

This reads as a genuine fitness gain across the board rather than one lucky split, since every leg improved rather than just one offsetting a weaker one elsewhere. I'm confident in this comparison since it's a direct same-distance, already-computed delta rather than an estimate.

One thing worth keeping in mind: these are different courses and conditions (different race, nearly a year apart), so some of the gap could be course-related rather than pure fitness — I don't have elevation or weather data to separate that out.

turns.message: Have I been improving year over year?
turns.reply:
Yes — the trend across your history is clearly upward, especially this year.

Looking at your repeated distances tells the story best. Your 70.3 went from 5:09:40 at Coastal (Sep 2025) to 4:58:50 at Ridgeline (Jun 2026) — almost 11 minutes faster, and every split improved: swim, bike, and run all came down, not just one lucky leg. Your 10K also improved, from 46:10 (Apr 2024) to 44:35 (Apr 2026), moving you from Top 7% to Top 5% overall. And your percentiles have generally been trending toward the stronger end — Harbor Sprint and Coastal 70.3 both sat around Top 14-17%, while your more recent Ridgeline 70.3 and Riverside 10K are Top 5-11%.

The pattern that stands out most: your most recent races (2026) are your best results across the board — PRs at the 70.3, 10K, and half marathon distances. That's a stronger signal than just "time passing" — it suggests real fitness gains, not just course variance, since the improvement shows up consistently across different disciplines and distances rather than in one isolated race.

I'm quite confident in this read since it's based on direct PR-to-PR and split-to-split comparisons rather than inference. One caveat: you don't have a lot of races per distance (two 70.3s, two 10Ks), so each data point carries real weight — a single bad-weather day or tough course could shift the picture more than it would with a longer history.

Within triathlon, swim is your relative standout — across your four triathlons, your swim consistently looks like the leg where you're punching above your overall placement, though run is close behind.

A cleaner way to see it: at Ridgeline 70.3, you finished Top 11% overall / Top 9% age group — and your swim-to-run pacing pattern (strong swim, solid bike, run that holds up rather than falls apart) shows up across Coastal 70.3, Lakeview Olympic, and Harbor Sprint too. Run in particular tends to hold position well late in the race (e.g., 1:41:30 off a 2:36 bike at Ridgeline), which is a good sign for an athlete moving toward full-distance racing.

But here's the catch if you mean "overall" rather than "within triathlon": you also have strong standalone running results — a 44:35 10K (Top 5% overall) and a 1:39:20 half marathon (Top 8% overall) — both better percentiles than any of your triathlon finishes. So if the question is about your overall racing ability across everything, not just triathlon legs, running has the stronger case, because that standalone evidence is both faster relatively and more consistent.

So: within triathlon, it's genuinely close between swim and run, with a slight lean toward swim as the leg where you over-perform most. Looking at everything you've raced, running is the stronger overall signal. I'm fairly confident in this since it's based on multiple consistent results, not a single race.

turns.message: Here is my long ride from last Saturday. What does it show?
turns.reply:
From your uploaded evidence: distance 92.4 km, time 2:42:10, avg power 188 W, normalized power 212 W, avg HR 148 bpm, max HR 171 bpm, Training Stress Score 168, elevation gain 1,120 m.

This looks like a solid, hilly aerobic-endurance ride rather than a flat-out effort, and it's a useful data point for your Desert IRONMAN prep.

A few things stand out. The gap between avg power (188 W) and normalized power (212 W) is fairly wide — about 13% — which usually means the effort was variable rather than steady, consistent with 1,120 m of climbing over the ride rather than a flat course. An avg HR of 148 with max of 171 suggests this was a moderate, sustainable aerobic effort, not a threshold-heavy session. The TSS of 168 for under 2:45 of riding is a meaningfully high training load, so this was a real endurance stimulus, not a recovery spin.

I can't directly compare this to your triathlon bike splits since those were raced efforts on different courses without power data recorded, and this was a training ride — so I'd be cautious drawing a direct "you're fitter now" conclusion from it alone. It's one solid long-ride data point, not a fitness verdict.

If you want this to actually inform your full-distance pacing plan, the most useful next pieces would be your FTP (or a recent power test) so I can translate 212 W NP into an intensity factor, and a few more long rides to see if this effort is typical or a standout.

Right now I can't really tell — there's only one race on record, so there's no trend to measure yet.

The Parkside 5K at 24:10 is your only completed result in RaceSignal (good for Top 33% overall and Top 35% in your age group, for what it's worth). "Getting faster" needs at least two results in the same or comparable distances to compare splits and pace over time, and that's not there yet.

If you've got an earlier 5K (or any race) that isn't in this history, tell me the time and date and I can compare it directly. Otherwise, the next 5K you run will be the first real data point to answer this — and if you've got a Garmin or Strava screenshot from a past race, I can pull useful numbers from that too even if it's not logged in RaceSignal.

turns.message: How much of my Ridgeline improvement came from my training volume and nutrition?
turns.reply:
I don't have any training volume or nutrition data to attribute your improvement to — RaceSignal only has race results and splits, not your training logs or fueling strategy, so I can't break the gap into "this much training, this much nutrition."

What I can tell you is what changed on race day, based on comparing Ridgeline 70.3 to your only other 70.3, Coastal 70.3: you were faster across every single split. Swim 50 seconds faster, bike 5:10 faster, run 4:30 faster, and both transitions 10 seconds quicker, adding up to a 10:50 overall improvement. The run holding up well after a stronger bike split is usually a good sign of either better aerobic fitness, better pacing, or better fueling on the bike (bonking less late in the ride tends to show up exactly like this) — but I genuinely can't tell you which of those it was without more information.

If you want to actually isolate nutrition's contribution, the things that would help most are: your bike power/pace data for both races to see if the bike itself was paced differently, your fueling log or notes from each race (carbs/hour, when you ate), and your run mile splits within each race to see if you faded less late in the run at Ridgeline. Without that, the honest answer is that the data shows you improved everywhere, but not why.

Your 10K PR is 44:35, from Riverside 10K on 2026-04-19.

That placed you in the Top 5% overall and Top 5% in your age group — your strongest percentile finish of any distance in your race history. For reference, you also ran 46:10 at the same race the year before (2024-04-20), so that's a 1:35 improvement year over year.

Ridgeline is your best 70.3 to date, finishing in 4:58:50 and good for Top 11% overall and Top 9% in your age group — a real step up from your only other 70.3.

Here's the shape of the race: Swim 35:50, T1 3:00, Bike 2:36:10, T2 2:20, Run 1:41:30. Compared to Coastal 70.3 (your first at this distance), every single split improved — swim 50s faster, bike 5m10s faster, run 4m30s faster, and both transitions tighter too. That's a clean, across-the-board improvement rather than one leg carrying the whole gain, which is a good sign of general fitness progress rather than a fluke.

Within this race itself, the run is the leg worth paying attention to. An hour-41 run off a 2:36 bike is a solid split, and paired with the fact that your run split gained the most time back versus Coastal (4m30s), it suggests your run durability off the bike is trending in the right direction — useful context given Desert IRONMAN is on your schedule.

I'd call this a strong, consistent performance with no obvious weak leg — I'm fairly confident in that read since it's backed by full splits and a direct same-distance comparison. What would sharpen it further is knowing your power/pace data from the bike (NP, IF) to see whether you paced it conservatively or redlined it, since that matters a lot for how this translates to a full-distance effort.

turns.message: Which leg gained the most compared with Coastal?
turns.reply:
The run gained the most — it was 4 minutes 30 seconds faster at Ridgeline than at Coastal 70.3, the largest improvement of any leg.

For comparison, the bike gained 5 minutes 10 seconds, which is actually the single biggest raw time gain — slightly more than the run in absolute terms. So if you're asking "which leg improved by the most time," that's the bike. But if you're thinking about it relative to how long each leg takes (run is roughly 1:41 vs. bike's 2:36), the run's gain represents a proportionally bigger jump in pace than the bike's does.

Swim and transitions improved too, but by much smaller amounts — 50 seconds on the swim, 10 seconds on each transition.

So: bike gained the most time outright (5m10s), run gained the most relative to its own length (4m30s off a shorter leg). Either way, nothing got worse — it was a clean improvement across the board. I'm confident in these numbers since they're directly from the precomputed comparison rather than anything I calculated myself.
